Ensure the work happens in an isolated workspace: use
superpowers:using-git-worktrees to create one or verify the existing one.
Never start implementation on a main/master branch without your human
partner's explicit consent.

Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions,
controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task
sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in
a ledger file, not only in todos.

- Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run this skill's
  `scripts/sdd-workspace PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's git-ignored
  directory (`<repo-root>/.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/`), home to
  every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages.
  Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write.
- Check for this plan's ledger at `<workspace>/progress.md`. If its first
  line names your plan file, tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE
  — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task
  whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next
  round. A ledger whose first line names a different plan file — or a stray
  ledger at the old flat path `.superpowers/sdd/progress.md` — is another
  plan's progress: leave it in place and start your own, fresh.
- Create the ledger with its identity as the first line:
  `# SDD ledger — plan: <plan file path>`.
- The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even
  when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction,
  trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- `git clean -fdx` will destroy the workspace (it's git-ignored scratch); if
  that happens, recover from `git log`.

Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a
todo per task.

Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts:

- tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints
- anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a
  defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block)

Present everything you find to your human partner as one batched question —
each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs —
before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. If the
scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for
conflicts that only emerge from implementation.

## Model Selection

Use the least powerful model that can handle each role to conserve cost and increase speed.

**Mechanical implementation tasks** (isolated functions, clear specs, 1-2 files): use a fast, cheap model. Most implementation tasks are mechanical when the plan is well-specified.

**Integration and judgment tasks** (multi-file coordination, pattern matching, debugging): use a standard model.

**Architecture and design tasks**: use the most capable available model.
The final whole-branch review is one of these — dispatch it on the most
capable available model, not the session default.

**Review tasks**: choose the model with the same judgment, scaled to the
diff's size, complexity, and risk. A small mechanical diff does not need the
most capable model; a subtle concurrency change does. Scoped re-reviews of
small fix diffs take a cheap-to-mid tier.

**Fix-loop escalation (rounds 4-5)**: use a model at least one tier above
the implementer that got stuck.

**Always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent.** An
omitted model inherits your session's model — often the most capable and
most expensive — which silently defeats this section.

**Turn count beats token price.** Wall-clock and context cost scale with how
many turns a subagent takes, and the cheapest models routinely take 2-3× the
turns on multi-step work — costing more overall. Use a mid-tier model as the
floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions.
When the task's plan text contains the complete code to write, the
implementation is transcription plus testing: use the cheapest tier for
that implementer. Single-file mechanical fixes also take the cheapest tier.

**Task complexity signals (implementation tasks):**
- Touches 1-2 files with a complete spec → cheap model
- Touches multiple files with integration concerns → standard model
- Requires design judgment or broad codebase understanding → most capable model

## The Task Loop

Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent
prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session
and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files.

### 1. Dispatch the implementer

Record BASE (`git rev-parse HEAD`) before dispatching — the review package
and fix-round diffs need it.

- **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's
  `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a
  uniquely named file and prints the path. Compose the dispatch so the
  brief stays the single source of
  requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this
  task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this
  first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim";
  (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot
  know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief;
  (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers,
  magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never
  make a subagent read the whole plan file.
- **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief
  (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in
  the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and
  returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns.
- A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not
  paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into
  later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99%
  was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it
  touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else.
- If an earlier task parked a finding in the area this task touches, carry
  a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch.
- Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result —
  fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent.
- Never dispatch multiple implementation subagents in parallel (conflicts).

Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md)

### 2. Handle the report

Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately:

**DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints the unique file path it wrote; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task), then dispatch the task reviewer with the printed path.

**DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review.

**NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch.

**BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker:
1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model
2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model
3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces
4. If the plan itself is wrong, escalate to the human

**Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change.

If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer
clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't
rush it into implementation.

### 3. Review the task

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` and pass the reviewer the file path
  it prints (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`,
  and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named
  file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop.
The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

### 4. The fix loop

The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important
finding, or a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap.

Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately:

- Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go
  (`Task <N>: minor (deferred): <one-liner>`), and point the final
  whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed
  before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings
  never enter the loop.
- A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with
  what the plan's text requires — is the human's decision, like any plan
  contradiction: present the finding and the plan text, ask which governs.
  Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not
  dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking.
Everything else enters the loop. A fix round is one fix dispatch plus one
scoped re-review. Five rounds maximum per task:

**Rounds 1-3 — resume the original implementer.** Send it the open findings
verbatim. Its context is intact: it knows the task, the code, and its own
choices. If your harness cannot send another message to a live subagent,
dispatch a fresh implementer carrying the brief path, the report-file path,
and the findings — the report file is the persistent memory either way.

**Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh implementer on a more capable model** (per
Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open
findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task
[N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop
that survives three resumes usually means the implementer cannot see its
own problem — fresh eyes and a capability bump in one move.

**Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests
covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file,
and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm
the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the
output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. Name the
covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the
whole suite.

**The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD`
where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the
brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts
each finding ADDRESSED or NOT ADDRESSED and flags new breakage in the fix
diff only. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open
findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred
minors — they never extend the loop.

**After each round,** append to the ledger:
`Task <N>: fix round <R>/5 (<X> addressed, <Y> open — <finding one-liners>; commits <a7>..<b7>)`

Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays
clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review.

**The breaker.** When round 5's re-review still leaves findings open, stop
dispatching. Adjudicate each open finding yourself — you hold the plan and
the cross-task context the reviewer lacks:

- **The reviewer is wrong, or the point is contestable:** park it —
  `Task <N>: parked — <finding> — ruling: <why the code stands>`. The final
  review sees both sides.
- **Real, but nothing downstream builds on it:** park it the same way, with
  a ruling that says it's real and deferred.
- **Real and load-bearing** — a later task builds on it, or it reveals a
  plan defect: STOP. Append `Task <N>: BLOCKED — <reason>` and report to
  your human partner with the finding, the plan text it collides with, and
  the fix history. Parking a structural failure lets every dependent task
  build on it and hands the final review a problem it cannot fix either.

Adjudicate only at the cap. Adjudicating earlier to end a loop is
pre-judging with a different name. Every adjudication is a ledger entry —
a silent discard is forbidden.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — or every open finding is parked with a
ruling at the cap — append the completion line to the ledger in the same
message as your other bookkeeping:

- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, review clean)`
- `Task <N>: complete (commits <base7>..<head7>, <K> parked)` after a
  tripped breaker

Then mark the todo complete and move on. Never move to the next task while
the review has open Critical/Important issues that are neither fixed nor
parked-with-ruling at the cap.

## Final Review

The final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) and include the
printed path in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads
one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
superpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor and parked lines so it can triage which must be
fixed before merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding.
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md)).
Adjudicate any residual findings as in the task loop's breaker: park with
rulings, or stop on load-bearing ones. There is no second fix wave —
residual load-bearing findings surface to your human partner when
finishing-a-development-branch presents the options.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged,
delete this plan's workspace (`rm -rf <workspace>`) — the git history is
the record now. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them
alone.

Use superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Close enough on spec compliance" | Reviewer found spec gaps = not done. Fix or hit the cap and adjudicate — those are the only exits. |
| "I'll fix it myself, dispatching is overhead" | Controller fixes pollute your context and skip review. Resume the implementer. |
| "One more round will converge" | Past the cap, rounds don't converge — the failure is structural. Adjudicate and route. |
| "The reviewer will just find something new anyway" | Scoped re-reviews verify fixes; they cannot wander. New findings on untouched code go to the ledger, not the loop. |
| "This finding is obviously wrong, I'll drop it" | You adjudicate only at the cap, and every ruling is a ledger entry. Silent discards are forbidden. |
| "The fix was small, skip the re-review" | Unreviewed fixes are how regressions land. Every round ends with a scoped re-review. |
| "Reviews slow the loop down" | The loop without reviews is just unverified churn. Reviews are the loop's brakes and steering. |
| "Ledger bookkeeping is overhead" | The ledger is what survives compaction. Controllers without one have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences. |

# Task 1 Review — `scripts/check.sh` (integrity check harness)

Verified by running the actual script against three constructed scenarios (not just reading the diff): the current repo state, a broken-link fixture at repo root, and a clean fixture with the five reference files entirely absent.

## Spec compliance: ❌ Not fully compliant

| Requirement | Verdict | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Catches placeholder text in shipped files, excludes `docs/` | ✅ | Regex covers all 7 terms; `docs/` correctly excluded. Verified: current repo's only placeholder hits all live under `docs/` and are correctly filtered. |
| `AGENTS.md` ≤ 200 lines | ✅ | `[ "$N" -le 200 ]` — correct boundary. Verified with fixture (3-line file → `ok`). |
| All 5 JSON adapter files validated as parseable | ✅ | `jq empty` on each named path; verified with fixture (`{}` files → all `ok: ... parses`). |
| Reference files checked for page-shaped **and** tool-shaped | ❌ | Only checked *if the file exists*. If missing, the loop body silently emits nothing — no `ok`, no `fail`. Verified by running the script against a fixture where AGENTS.md/JSON/frontmatter/links all pass but `STYLES.md`, `CRAFT.md`, `TOOLS.md`, `SURFACES.md`, `ACCESS.md` don't exist at all: the script printed **`ALL CHECKS PASS`, exit 0**. |
| `SURFACES.md` asserted to carry 44+28 as a pair | ❌ | Same missing-file silent-skip bug (see above — this block has the identical structural flaw). Additionally, even when the file exists, the check is `grep -q '44' && grep -q '28'` — two independent substring tests, not a pairing check (see Important #1 below). |
| Exit 0 clean / 1 on violation | ✅ | Verified both exit codes directly (0 in the missing-reference-file fixture — which is itself the bug; 1 in every real-failure scenario tested). |

## Task quality: findings (Critical → Minor)

### Critical — reference-file checks silently no-op when the file is missing
**File:** `scripts/check.sh`, lines ~62–76 (both the "every reference file forks on surface class" loop and the "Apple numbers ship as pairs" block).

Every other check in the script has an explicit `else fail "$f missing"` (AGENTS.md, all 5 JSON files, all 3 frontmatter files). These two blocks don't:

```bash
for f in STYLES.md CRAFT.md TOOLS.md SURFACES.md ACCESS.md; do
  if [ -f "$f" ]; then
    ...
  fi   # <-- no else fail "$f missing"
done
```

**Failure scenario, empirically reproduced:** I built a fixture directory with a valid `AGENTS.md` (3 lines), 5 valid JSON files, 3 valid frontmatter files, and zero broken links — but deliberately did **not** create `STYLES.md`/`CRAFT.md`/`TOOLS.md`/`SURFACES.md`/`ACCESS.md`. Running the shipped `check.sh` against it printed:
```
== every reference file forks on surface class ==
== Apple numbers ship as pairs ==

ALL CHECKS PASS
```
Exit code `0`. This is the exact "false confidence" failure mode the review brief warned about for the link check — except here it's real. Given this 15-task build almost certainly creates `AGENTS.md`/adapters/frontmatter before it creates the reference docs (a later task), there is a real window in this build where the harness will report clean while five required files don't exist yet.

This bug is present verbatim in `task-1-brief.md` (the implementer did not introduce it — confirmed via diff against the brief, the only change is the `.superpowers/` exclusion). But the implementer's own report captures the blank output under these two headers and doesn't flag it, despite testing the script directly and being the one AGENTS charged with treating this script as everyone else's safety net.

### Important — "Apple numbers ship as pairs" check doesn't actually check pairing
**File:** `scripts/check.sh`, line ~73: `grep -q '44' SURFACES.md && grep -q '28' SURFACES.md`

This tests independent presence of the substrings `44` and `28` anywhere in the file — not that they're stated together as a default+minimum pair. **Failure scenario:** `SURFACES.md` could repeat the exact myth the brief guards against ("Apple's minimum tap target is 44pt", no mention of 28 anywhere near it) and still pass, as long as `28` appears anywhere else in the document for an unrelated reason (a line count, a WCAG figure, a year, a version). Conversely two coincidental, unrelated occurrences of `44` and `28` anywhere in a long doc would satisfy it. This weakens the "never 44 alone" guarantee the brief explicitly calls out.

### Important — inconsistent scratch-directory exclusion causes real false-positive noise, demonstrated live
Implementer added `.superpowers/` exclusion to the placeholder scan but not to the internal-link check. **Reproduced without any setup on my part:** running `./scripts/check.sh` on the untouched repo right now reports:
```
FAIL: broken link in ./.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-01-inter-face-build/task-1-report.md -> ./nonexistent-file.md
FAIL: broken link in ./.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-01-inter-face-build/task-1-report.md -> ./missing.md
```
These come from the implementer's own report, which quotes example broken-link markdown inside a code fence while documenting their test — the link checker doesn't distinguish code fences from real links. I confirmed `.superpowers/sdd/` is genuinely git-ignored scratch (`.superpowers/sdd/.gitignore` contains a bare `*`, itself untracked/self-ignoring — `git check-ignore` confirms it). So this is noise, not a real defect, but it means the harness currently cannot report clean on the actual working tree, and will keep crying wolf every time a future task report documents link-check examples in prose — training whoever reads the output to ignore FAILs, which is the opposite of what a gate script should do.

### Minor — `.superpowers/` exclusion is broader than what's proven ignored
The exclusion (`grep -v '^\./\.superpowers/'`) covers all of `.superpowers/`, but only `.superpowers/sdd/` has been shown to be git-ignored. If a future task ever places tracked/shipped content directly under `.superpowers/` outside `sdd/`, the placeholder scan would blind itself to it. Scoping the exclusion to `.superpowers/sdd/` would match the actual ignore boundary at no extra cost. That said — the core judgment call (exclude it, it's scratch not shipped) is correct, not a blind spot in the way the review brief worried about.

### Minor — hand-maintained exclusion lists, not git-aware (architectural note)
`docs/`, `.git`, `.superpowers/` are each manually hardcoded per-check. The repo's own `.gitignore` already reserves `runs/*/` and `.gstack/` (currently present, currently inert but real — `.gstack/*.json` exists today). Any future git-ignored scratch dir needs the same manual exclusion added to *every* check doing a raw filesystem grep, or it produces exactly the kind of noise/blind-spot pair seen above. `git ls-files -- '*.md' '*.json' '*.mdc' | xargs grep ...` would be self-maintaining and correctly scoped to "shipped" by construction — this is the lazier fix, not a bigger one. Not asked for in the brief, so not a defect in what was delivered, just worth flagging for a later cleanup pass.

### Verified correct, not a finding — the convoluted link-check block works
I ran the two required experiments directly:
1. Created `definitely-not-here-source.md` at repo root with `[broken link](./definitely-not-here-xyz.md)` → `./scripts/check.sh` reported `FAIL: broken link in ./definitely-not-here-source.md -> ./definitely-not-here-xyz.md`.
2. Deleted the file, re-ran → that specific FAIL disappeared.

The implementer's claim ("the redundancy doesn't affect correctness") is **confirmed true**. The first `grep -rhoE ... | grep -v ... >/dev/null 2>&1` is genuinely dead code — its output is discarded — so it just doubles the filesystem scan for nothing. Waste, not a bug. Should have been deleted rather than left in (a one-line diff), but leaving it isn't a correctness problem.

### Verified safe — `set -uo pipefail`
No `set -e` is present, so non-zero exit codes never abort the script outright; `pipefail` only changes what `$?` reports for a given pipeline. Every place that matters is already guarded: the placeholder-scan pipeline ends in `|| true`; the JSON/frontmatter checks use explicit `&&`/`||`; the link-check pipeline feeds an unchecked process substitution (`while ... done < <(...)`, whose exit status bash doesn't wait on in this idiom). No unset-variable references were found under `set -u`. This combination is safe given the script's structure.

## Bottom line
The implementer's one deliberate change (`.superpowers/` exclusion) is directionally correct and independently verified against `.gitignore`. The link-check block, despite looking suspicious, was correctly verified as functional by running it, not just reading it. But the review surfaced a genuine Critical defect the implementer's own test output exposed and didn't investigate: two of the seven checks (reference-file surface-class coverage, and the SURFACES.md 44/28 pair assertion) are complete no-ops when their target files don't exist, which I reproduced as a false `ALL CHECKS PASS` / exit 0. Since this script is the sole gate for the remaining 14 tasks, that gap should be closed (add the missing `else fail` branches) before treating Task 1 as done.

## Review: Task 2 — PRINCIPLES.md

### Spec compliance: ✅

All hard constraints verified directly, not assumed:

1. **`./scripts/check.sh`** — ran it. Output is byte-for-byte the same failure set as Task 1's recorded baseline (missing `AGENTS.md`, 5 JSON adapters, 3 frontmatter files, `STYLES.md`/`CRAFT.md`/`TOOLS.md`/`SURFACES.md`/`ACCESS.md`). Placeholder scan: `ok: no placeholders`. Link check: `ok: all relative links resolve`. Confirmed independently with `grep -nE '\]\(' PRINCIPLES.md` → zero matches — no markdown links anywhere, all seven not-yet-built files (`ACCESS.md`, `STYLES.md`, `CRAFT.md`, `TOOLS.md`, `TRANSLATE.md`, `DIRECTION.md`, `tokens.json`) are referenced only as backtick code spans.

2. **16 rules, 3 [HARD]** — `grep -cE '^## [0-9]+\.'` → 16. `[HARD` occurs 5 times total, but only 3 are rule markers: line 80 (§10), line 138 (§15), line 158 (§16). The other two are the intro sentence ("Three of them are **hard**...") and the phrase "non-**[HARD]** step" inside §16's body — not new markers. Exactly the right three.

3. **§-mapping** — cross-checked all 14 carried rows against the brief's table (all 14 match by name and content: §5←pf.me§7 "The work is the hero", §7←pf.me§9 "Own every asset", §14←pf.me§22 likeness, etc.) and additionally cross-checked against every live `§`-reference in `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-inter-face-build.md` (lines 534, 646, 696, 748, 758, 988, etc. — ACCESS.md consumes §10/§15, BREAKING.md marks §10/§15/§16 unbreakable, surface-designer cites §9 for image text, vendoring cites §7). Every forward reference lines up. Internal cross-refs inside the file were also correctly renumbered (§14 correctly points to `§8` for "generate every visual" and `§10` for alt text, matching pf.me's §22→§10/§12 originals).

4. **§9 rewrite** — genuine. Fully retargeted from page-copy rules ("em-dash cadence," "the way the subject talks," `BRIEF.md` lexicon) to image-text rules (realistic copy lengths, minimal text per image, no invented brand names, lorem-free domain-appropriate placeholder). Matches the brief's specified text verbatim. This does not read as a rule about page copy.

5. **§10 rewrite** — the opening (structural finding, verbatim from brief) and closing (Loop 1, `ACCESS.md`, "before a single image generates") genuinely reframe the rule as design-time. See Minor finding below for a caveat on the middle paragraph.

6. **Generalization quality** — consistently specific, not flattened. "the subject or product," "TRANSLATE.md's three-second feel" (concrete file pointer replacing the dropped "vision" concept), "screen transitions," "broken interface," "It builds is not it renders." No instance of vague filler like "be thoughtful about accessibility."

### Task quality: Approved, with 1 Minor finding

**Minor — §9 breaks its own "subject or product" pattern.**
- **File:** `PRINCIPLES.md`, line 78 (§9).
- **What's wrong:** Every other generalized reference to the entity being designed for uses "subject or product" (§1 line 18, §3 line 30, §6 line 52, §13 line 112). §9 alone reverts to "the subject's actual domain" instead of "the subject or product's actual domain."
- **Consequence:** Cosmetic only — "domain" still reads sensibly for a pure product with no human subject — but it's a small inconsistency in an otherwise carefully generalized document, and this is exactly the kind of file ten other tasks will pattern-match against.

**Observation, not a finding:** §10's middle paragraph (semantic structure, alt text, contrast, reduced-motion, WebGL fallback) is carried over from portfolio.me §12 almost verbatim, lightly reworded ("Semantic HTML" → "Semantic structure or platform-native components"). The brief asked for a rule that is "design-time, not a checklist" — the bookending paragraphs (structural finding at the top, Loop-1/`ACCESS.md` mandate at the bottom) do accomplish that reframing, and the brief's required verbatim text is present and correctly placed. I don't rate this a spec failure since the brief didn't forbid keeping concrete requirements, but if I were nitpicking the tightest possible read of "not a checklist," the middle paragraph is where a reviewer's eye would catch on. Judgment call, not a defect.

No Critical or Important findings. The mapping, the two required rewrites, the hard-rule count, and the no-links constraint all check out against the actual repo state, not just the report's claims.

- **Dangling refs:** `grep -n 'DOMAIN\.md\|ARCHITECTURE\.md\|Gate C\|Gate D' TOOLS.md` returns nothing. All three systemcicy-only doc reaches are gone, substance retained where it existed independent of the citation.

No new failures, `ok: no placeholders`, `grep -nE '\]\(' TOOLS.md` returns nothing (no markdown links).
- **§ citations:** all five (`§11`, `§15`×2, `§10`) resolve to real rules in this repo's 16-rule `PRINCIPLES.md`; none point at a wrong or unrelated rule (see escalated call 2 below for the one stretch).

## Task quality: one Important finding, otherwise strong

**Important — `TOOLS.md` lines 106-117, "Desktop window states" table, the Main row is factually wrong, contradicting its own cited source.**

The row claims: *"Main | The window someone is working in. Content and controls read as fully live."*

But the source it's built from, `docs/research/tablet-desktop-verified.md:116-118`, quotes Apple's own documentation directly: the key window *"uses color in the title bar options for closing, minimizing, and zooming; **inactive windows and main windows that aren't key use gray**."* That is: a window that is Main but not Key — a real, common case (a document window stays main while a Find panel or inspector becomes key) — shows the *same gray controls as Inactive*. The shipped table's own Key row ("controls render in color... only when...") and Inactive row ("chrome... grays out") both correctly reflect this. Only the Main row contradicts the source three lines above it in the same research doc, and contradicts its own table's other two rows. Since this table is prescriptive "what it must do" design guidance in a project whose explicit bar for this exact content class is "quotes verified against source, 0 fabrications" (per `progress.md` Task 4/5), this is a real accuracy defect, not a nitpick — it could lead an implementer to build the Main-vs-Key visual distinction backwards.

**Failure scenario:** someone building a desktop-shaped tool with a main document window and a separate floating inspector panel reads this table, ships colored/"live" window controls on the main window even when an inspector has stolen key focus, and never notices the discrepancy from Apple's actual HIG behavior — because the file told them it was correct.

Everything else checked out clean: the §-renumbering table's mappings all independently verified against `PRINCIPLES.md`'s actual 16 rules; the three doc-ref removals are substance-preserving; the STYLES.md-pointer paragraph is inserted without disturbing the original section-12 content; the trunk-test citation (`docs/audit/competitor-small-skills.md:350`) is accurate, word-for-word. Report is honest and specific about its own judgment calls rather than concealing them.

## The three escalated calls

**1. Dropping `§9`/`§25`/`§7` bare citations — RIGHT.** I checked all three independently against `PRINCIPLES.md`'s 16 rules myself, not just the report's table. This repo's `§9` is "anti-slop, aimed at what the images say" (scoped to image-generated text — already established narrowly in Task 4), unrelated to "every state is designed." No principle here covers UX copywriting/system's-words as a general concept (`§25`'s target). No principle covers authorization or a security check (`§7`'s target) — correct, since this plugin has no backend or runtime to enforce anything server-side. Forcing any of the three would have produced a misleading citation, which the brief itself says is worse than none. Dropping was correct on all three.

**2. `§10` for "never color alone" — acceptable stretch, not misleading.** `§10` ("Accessible by default **[HARD]**") is written as a non-exhaustive umbrella — it explicitly says "the full decision list... lives in `ACCESS.md`" — rather than a closed enumeration. "Never rely on color alone" is a standard, well-known accessibility rule that sits squarely under that umbrella even though `§10`'s own text doesn't spell it out verbatim. A reader following the citation lands on the correct general rule (hard accessibility), not a wrong one. Same category as the Task 5 icon-grade precedent cited in the report. I'd rule this fine as shipped, correctly self-flagged rather than passed off as a verbatim match.

**3. Section 13 restructuring — coherent.** Verified independently against the actual plan doc (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-01-inter-face-build.md:704`, "`DIRECTION.md` at rendered-style resolution" is established terminology from the plan itself, not invented for this task) and against `PRINCIPLES.md §16` (exactly two gates, A and B — no Gate C/D exist in this repo). **Minor**

**The paraphrase is not an acceptable loss.** I tested both patterns:

```
'…|FIXME|XXX'    on "xSmall through xxxLarge"  → MATCHES (false positive confirmed)
'…|FIXME|\bXXX\b' on "xSmall through xxxLarge"  → no match  (fixed)
'\bXXX\b' still catches: "value: XXX" ✅  "also xxx here" ✅  "foo XXX-bar" ✅
```

One word-boundary pair. **Zero detection lost** — every real placeholder form still trips, including lowercase `xxx` standalone. Against that, the current cost is real: `xxxLarge` is precisely the kind of citable string this file exists to hold, and "from xSmall up to the largest standard step" does not tell the reader *what the largest standard step is called* — the ramp is now unusable as a reference without going back to Apple. The scope-creep argument also cuts the right way: `ACCESS.md` writes the same ramp and hits the identical wall, so the paraphrase is a per-file tax, not a one-off.

Patch (`scripts/check.sh`, placeholder scan line):
```
-  'example\.com|\bTBD\b|\bTODO\b|Lorem ipsum|test claim|FIXME|XXX' \
+  'example\.com|\bTBD\b|\bTODO\b|Lorem ipsum|test claim|FIXME|\bXXX\b' \
```
Then restore `SURFACES.md:239–240` to Apple's actual ramp: *seven standard, xSmall through xxxLarge with Large as the default*. I did not apply either change — reviewer, not implementer.

Nothing here is ⚠️ unverifiable; the diff is a single new file and I checked everything against the working tree.

You are implementing Task 8 of the `inter.face` build. inter.face is a cross-agent design plugin made of markdown; an agent reads it and follows it, there is no runtime.

This task writes `ACCESS.md` — the file that exists because of the project's central audit finding, and it does its own research first.

**Read this first — your requirements, with exact values verbatim:**
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-01-inter-face-build/task-8-brief.md`

**Why this file exists.** The three parent pipelines all marked accessibility a HARD rule, and across ~5,000 lines contained **zero** mentions of ARIA, focus management, live regions, or accessible names. Not an oversight — a structural consequence of only ever *checking* accessibility in a final pass, never *designing* it. Everything in this file is a Loop 1 decision, made before an image is generated. Open with that claim; it is the file's reason for being.

**Your verified sources:**
- `docs/research/accessibility-wcag.md` — WCAG 2.2's six new A/AA criteria, WCAG 3.0 status
- `docs/research/web-a11y-patterns.md` — ARIA APG pattern commitments, WebAIM Million data
- `docs/research/native-a11y-verified.md` — Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Android scaling
- `docs/research/platform-numbers-verified.md` — contrast boundaries, the 200% rule
- `docs/research/icons-verified.md` — icon accessibility

Grep the rendered text rather than dumping whole pages. Write findings to `docs/research/legal-and-focus-verified.md` in the same header style as the other research docs.

**THE RULE THAT MATTERS MOST HERE:** if a fact does not verify, **write "not established in this pass — verify before relying on it"** rather than guessing. A wrong compliance deadline in a design tool is worse than an absent one — someone could rely on it. This project has already caught four instances of plausible-but-wrong content, including one claim that contradicted its own cited source. Do not add a fifth, and legal content is where it would do the most damage.

**Then write `ACCESS.md`.** The brief specifies the sections. Highlights that must land:
- **WCAG 2.2's six new A/AA criteria as design decisions** — 2.5.8 target size (24×24 CSS px effective, satisfiable by size OR the geometric spacing exception — `SURFACES.md` defers the spacing geometry to you, so give it), 2.5.7 dragging (a visible non-drag pointer affordance; keyboard support does NOT satisfy it), 2.4.11 focus not obscured, 3.3.8 accessible authentication, 3.3.7, 3.2.6.
- **WCAG 2.2 AA is the operative target** — 3.0 is a Working Draft (3 March 2026) that says it has "several years of work" left and does not deprecate WCAG 2.
- **ARIA pattern choice is a design decision** — grid vs table is a keyboard-model commitment (a grid exposes exactly ONE focusable element to the tab sequence; every focusable element in a table stays in it). Combobox forces a closed choice of four popup roles. Menu/menubar: Tab *exits*, arrows navigate. Modal dialog bundles focus trap + bidirectional transfer + content-dependent initial focus. Note the disclosure-vs-accordion boundary is contested (open W3C issue, no editor resolution).
- **The measured case:** WebAIM Million 2026, ~1M pages — pages using ARIA average **59.1 detected errors vs 42 without (~41% more)**, scaling with attribute count; of pages using `role="menu"`, **22% actively introduce barriers**. An ARIA role is "a promise" carrying no native keyboard behavior.

Diff is exactly two new files, nothing else touched.

---

### Claim 1: "The EAA never names WCAG at all" — **correct, and it contradicts the commentary**

I pulled the full consolidated Directive (EU) 2019/882 from EUR-Lex. Confirmed the fetch was complete, not a shell: `Whereas:` recitals present, Articles 1–33 present, `ANNEX I` through `ANNEX VI` all present.

```
grep -ic "WCAG"                     → 0
grep -i  "Web Content Accessibility" → 0
grep -i  "W3C"                       → 0
grep -i  "301 549" / "ETSI"          → 0
```

Article 15 ("Presumption of conformity") reads exactly as `ACCESS.md` quotes it — conformity is *presumed* for products and services conforming to harmonised standards whose references are published in the OJEU. `ACCESS.md:1224`'s conclusion is right: **"Any sentence of the form 'the EAA requires WCAG 2.1 AA' is a two-step inference presented as a citation."** Confirming this is worth the pass — it is the opposite of what most secondary commentary says.

One detail that raises my confidence in the implementer's judgment rather than lowering it: `legal-and-focus-verified.md:124` writes the chain as "EAA → harmonised standard **(EN 301 549)** → WCAG". That parenthetical is itself an unverified inference — the directive never names EN 301 549. **`ACCESS.md:1223` dropped it.** The shipped file is more conservative than its own research doc. That is the correct direction for a leak to run.

### Claim 2: DOJ April 2026 extension — **correct, verbatim**

ada.gov returns the exact sentence `ACCESS.md:1231-1237` quotes:

> On April 20, 2026, the Federal Register published the Department's Interim Final Rule (IFR) extending the compliance date for State and local government entities with a total population of 50,000 or more to **April 26, 2027**. The compliance date for public entities with a total population of less than 50,000, or any special district government, is extended to **April 26, 2028**.

Also confirmed on the same page: WCAG 2.1 Level AA as the technical standard; the parking-app contractor example verbatim; DOJ naming WCAG 3.0 as a hypothetical acceptable higher standard.

---

## Honesty of the unverified list — **confirmed, all three**

| Claimed unestablished | Grep result in `ACCESS.md` |
|---|---|
| EN 301 549 edition | `301 549\|ETSI\|v3.2.1\|v4.1.1` → **only** lines 1262 and 1342, both "not established in this pass". §12's chain stops at "harmonised standard" and does not complete to a WCAG version. Zero confident assertions. |
| Cross-screen-reader live-region behaviour | `NVDA\|JAWS` → **only** lines 759 and 1337, both disclaimers. The other six `VoiceOver` hits are Apple-native grouping/label/alt-text claims, none about live regions. "Must exist in the DOM before injection" appears **only as a negation** (757, 1335). |
| SPA route-change focus | §6 names it a specification gap, requires the decision, supplies no destination. **More conservative than the report describes** — the practitioner answers (`tabindex="-1"` heading, `main`, skip link, route announcer) stayed in the research doc and were not carried into the shipped file at all. |

No leak in any of the three. One unrelated leak found — see Minor 1.

- **Six new A/AA criteria** all present as decisions: 2.5.8, 2.5.7, 2.4.11, 3.3.8, 3.3.7, 3.2.6.
- **2.5.8 spacing geometry** (`SURFACES.md:161` defers, `ACCESS.md:119-142` delivers): 24 px circle, no-intersection rule, plus three consequences (24 px centre-to-centre, diagonal failure, neighbour's box not its circle) — each labeled as derivation, not quotation. Correct handling.
- **17 pt contrast boundary** — `SURFACES.md:284-286` hands off, `ACCESS.md` §3 carries the full Apple table with the "iOS body is 17 pt, on the strict side" consequence. ✅
- **Reduce Transparency / Increase Contrast** — `SURFACES.md:61,353,538` defer, `ACCESS.md` §10 delivers a three-state table. ✅
- **WebAIM Million, verified live at webaim.org/projects/million/**: "59.1 on average… 42 on average" ✅; "5.7% of home pages had an ARIA menu… 22% of those ARIA menus introduced accessibility barriers" ✅. ### Important 1 — one unhedged universal in the legal claim

`ACCESS.md:70`:

> **And no law in force names 2.2 either** (§12 below).

§12 gets the same claim right at line 1187: *"**No instrument verified here** names WCAG 2.2."* And the file's own unverified list, item 5, says: *"Any jurisdiction outside the US and EU. Not researched at all."*

So §1 asserts globally what §12 correctly scopes to three instruments. It's self-correcting two sections later and the design conclusion (2.2 is anticipatory, not compliance) is unaffected — but this is precisely the verified/remembered blur the project has been fighting, sitting in its highest-damage section. One-word fix: *"no law **verified here** names 2.2 either."*

### Minor 1 — the one leak, and it's in the SPA section

`ACCESS.md:672`:

> The default, in most frameworks, is that focus falls to `<body>`

Unattributed empirical claim about framework behaviour. Not in the provenance table; `grep -rniE "falls to .body|activeElement" docs/research/*.md` returns nothing. It happens to be true, but it is stated bare in the one section whose entire argument is that this area is unspecified. Hedge it or drop it.

### Minor 2 — report-only, no file impact

Report unverified-item 6 says the practitioner answers "are named as *not* being in any spec read" in the shipped file. They aren't named at all. The report's "and/or `legal-and-focus-verified.md`" phrasing technically covers it. Noting only because the shipped file is stricter than its own description — the safe direction.

**No Critical findings.**

---

## Ruling on size: **earned — do not split, and §12 is the wrong seam anyway**

Section line counts:

| §2 six criteria | §4 ARIA | §11 i18n | §10 native | §12 **the law** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **240** | 168 | 141 | 118 | **109** |

§12 is the *fifth*-largest section. Splitting it saves 8% of the file and buys a second file, a cross-link, and a sync obligation — the worst trade available. The implementer's instinct that §12 is the cleanest *conceptual* seam is right; it just isn't a size lever.

The real test is whether §12 is read on a different occasion from the rest. It isn't: §1 forward-references §12 explicitly at line 70, and a run asking "what is my accessibility target" reads them together. Splitting would break the one cross-reference that matters.

And the file is read on demand — `check.sh`'s resident budget check tests `AGENTS.md`, not this. 1,357 lines costs nothing at idle.

Density holds up under inspection: 240 lines carrying six criteria with normative quotes, five named exceptions, two scope corrections, and a geometry derivation is not padding. **Nothing should split or go.** If a budget ever forces a cut, the honest target is §2's per-criterion prose, not §12 — and I would argue against that too.

input.prompt:
You are implementing Task 9 of the `inter.face` build — two files, one assembled from audit findings and one **authored from scratch**. inter.face is a cross-agent design plugin made of markdown; an agent reads it and follows it, there is no runtime.

Working directory: `/Users/taha/Documents/inter.face` (git branch `build/plugin-files`).

**Read this first — your requirements:**
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-01-inter-face-build/task-9-brief.md`

**Already built, read for consistency:** `PRINCIPLES.md` (cite `§N` backticked, by real numbers), `TRANSLATE.md` (rows), `STYLES.md` (families, and it already references both of your files).

---

## `REDESIGN.md` — assembled, four steps

Source: `docs/audit/competitor-small-skills.md` §3 has the full method extraction. The composite exists in neither source alone:

1. **Extract the rendered system** — gstack design-review's DOM queries (fonts actually in use, the real palette, heading scale, every interactive element under 44px) plus a perf read. Output is a `CURRENT.md`: what the surface *is* today, measured, not described.
2. **Position it against `STYLES.md`** — which family is it closest to, and is that a choice or an accident? A site 80% one family is that family with drift. A site that is 30% of six families has no position. Different problems, different fixes.
3. **Classify the ask — a FORK, not a slider.** *Correction* (position right, execution drifted) runs an audit and fix-priority pass against the extracted system. *Reposition* (the position itself is wrong) runs Loop 1 with `CURRENT.md` as a constraint, plus the question greenfield never asks: **what is load-bearing and must survive?** — which is exactly `TRANSLATE.md` row 6.
4. **Fix Priority ladder** — order by impact ÷ risk, not by category. Font swap first (largest visible delta, smallest blast radius); typography polish last. An audit without an order is a backlog; with an order it is a plan.

State the discipline the small skill lacks and gstack has: **one fix at a time, re-screenshot after each, classify verified / best-effort / reverted, and a hard cap.** A scan-diagnose-fix pass with no gate and no revert path is more dangerous than the problem it solves.

---

## `BREAKING.md` — **authored, not researched**

No primary source publishes "when to violate design conventions." Do not go looking for one and do not pad this with citations that do not exist. It is the natural completion of `§1`–`§3`, which currently say *be bold* and then hand the agent a rulebook — a contradiction the parent pipelines never resolved.

**Structure per breakable rule:** what it is · what breaking it buys · what it costs · the conditions that make the trade honest · how to record it.

Cover at least these, with real conditions rather than platitudes:
- **Platform convention** (a non-native nav, a custom control). Buys distinctiveness; costs learnability and every affordance the platform gave you free. Honest when the audience uses this daily and the gain compounds; dishonest on a one-visit surface.
- **The category cliché fence** — sometimes the cliché is load-bearing (a padlock on a bank). Breaking *the fence* means using the expected form **deliberately**, which is a different act from reaching for it reflexively. Record which one it was.
- **Density norms** — a marketing page that goes dense, a tool that goes spacious. Honest when the content genuinely inverts the usual read pattern.
- **A style's own guardrails** — shipping a named style unmodified is a `§3` failure, but deliberately shipping it near-pure *as the collision itself* is legitimate if stated.
- **The two-tier performance budget** — a heavy hero that blows the shell budget, when the surface's whole job is proving capability.

**The never-breakable list, with one line each on why:** `§10` accessibility, `§15` keyboard completeness on tool-shaped surfaces, `§16` the human gates, and **`TRANSLATE.md` row 5 (anti-positioning)**. The unifying reason: breaking these transfers cost onto someone who did not consent. That is a different category from an aesthetic risk the designer absorbs themselves.

**The recording rule:** a broken rule that is not written down is indistinguishable from a mistake. Every break is named in `DIRECTION.md` with its rationale and its cost. That is what separates a decision from an accident, and it is what `§3`'s "name what was invented" was always reaching for.

---

**CARRIED CONSTRAINT from Task 4:** `STYLES.md` already promises in prose that `BREAKING.md`'s never-breakable list contains `TRANSLATE.md` row 5 alongside `§10`/`§15`/`§16`. All four must be there or `STYLES.md` is left lying.

```js
return [s.color, s.backgroundColor, s.borderTopColor];
```

My stub's single H1 — one red text color, zero borders — returned `'rgb(255, 0, 0)': 2`. On a real page, text colors are inflated 2:1 over backgrounds, so the body text color will out-rank the page background even where the background paints a thousand times the area. The output is a census of *computed values*, not of *painted* ones.
2. **It isn't ranked.** The `reduce` returns an insertion-ordered object. A human has to sort it by eye.

Both are one-line fixes: gate the border color on `parseFloat(s.borderTopWidth) > 0`, and append `Object.entries(m).sort((a,b) => b[1]-a[1])`.

This matters more than a normal typo because the ranked palette feeds step 2's "~80% of one family" reading, which is the input to the step-3 fork. 1. **`REDESIGN.md:69–73` — the palette one-liner contradicts its own label, twice.** Double-counts text color via the default `borderTopColor`; returns an unsorted object despite "ranked" appearing in both the code comment and the table row. Demonstrated by execution. Two one-line fixes. Full detail above.

**Minor**

2. **`REDESIGN.md:80–83` — the sub-44 sweep's noise sources aren't named.** `getBoundingClientRect()` returns 0×0 for `display:none`, so every closed dropdown, hidden menu item, and unmounted modal control lands in the results; `[tabindex]` additionally catches `tabindex="-1"` programmatic focus targets that aren't interactive. The "44 is a net, not the law / adjudicate each hit" guard covers this in spirit but doesn't name it, and an agent that doesn't know will report the raw count.

3. **`BREAKING.md:212` — the only non-verbatim quoted string in either file.** Renders `§3`'s requirement as `"what this run did that nobody else does"`; both `PRINCIPLES.md:33-34` and `STYLES.md:516` say *"what it did to the style that nobody else does."* Meaning preserved, internal reference, no fabrication — but it's inside quotation marks and it's the one string that doesn't survive `grep -F`.

6. **`scripts/check.sh:52` — the fork check hardcodes five filenames.** `REDESIGN.md` and `BREAKING.md` aren't in the loop, so "both open addressing page-shaped and tool-shaped" is now an unenforced convention for the two newest files. Same shape as the Task 4 constraint that was honored here. ⚠️ Cannot verify until those tasks land.

**Verdict: Approved with one Important fix.** Land finding 1 before this is treated as final; 2–6 are cleanup. content.text:
All checks complete. Here are the two verdicts.

---

# Spec compliance: ✅

Every item in the brief is present.

**REDESIGN.md** — all four steps, in order, with the required content: extraction → `CURRENT.md` (5 recoveries + perf read); positioning against `STYLES.md` with the 80%/30% readings; the correction/reposition fork; the impact÷risk ladder. The discipline paragraph the brief demanded (one fix at a time, re-screenshot after each, classify verified/best-effort/reverted, hard cap) is all present as §5 rules 1–4, and the brief's closing line survives near-verbatim at REDESIGN.md:298.

**BREAKING.md** — five-field structure, all five breakable rules the brief named, the never-breakable four, the consent rationale, the recording rule with the `DIRECTION.md` tie-back to `§3`.

`./scripts/check.sh`: 9 FAILs, all `missing` for files owned by later tasks (`AGENTS.md`, 5 manifests, 3 skill/command/rule files). Zero new failures. Placeholder scan, link resolution, fork checks, Apple pairing all ok. Report's characterization is accurate.

**Convention checks, all pass:**
- `grep -oE '\(§[0-9]+\)'` → empty
- Zero markdown links in either file (all 10 file references backticked, including unbuilt `CURRENT.md`, `DIRECTION.md`, `loops/01-direction.md`)
- Zero placeholders
- Every backticked `§N` (1,2,3,7,10,11,12,15,16) resolves to a real PRINCIPLES.md rule; every bare `§N` is a self-reference with `above`/`below`. Clean separation.
- Both files open on the page-shaped/tool-shaped fork before any other content (REDESIGN.md:14, BREAKING.md:22)

**One deviation:** the brief said "typography polish last." REDESIGN.md's page-shaped ladder puts spacing/typography polish at rung 6 and "the signature move" at rung 7. Deliberate and justified in-file (it inverts to first on a reposition), disclosed in the provenance table. Noted, not a failure.

---

# Quote integrity: ✅ both files

**REDESIGN.md — all 8 verbatim blocks `grep -F` verified against `docs/audit/competitor-small-skills.md`.** I checked all eight, not five:

| # | Quote | Audit line |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | the `$B js` fonts query | 116 |
| 2 | "Font swap — biggest instant improvement, lowest risk" | 67 |
| 3 | "Polish typography scale and spacing — the premium final touch" | 68 |
| 4 | "Do not break existing functionality. Test after every change" | 278 |
| 5–8 | the four host rules | 269–272 |

Zero fabrications. The provenance table at REDESIGN.md:306–310 is honest about the seam — I re-derived it from audit §3 (lines 236–291) and it matches, including the audit's own admission that the composite method is assembled rather than sourced.

Cross-file claims also verified rather than trusted: `SURFACES.md` really does carry WCAG 2.5.8's 24×24, the 48dp/44pt pair, and Apple's 28pt-vs-44pt distinction exactly as REDESIGN.md:86–89 states; `TOOLS.md` §4's nine states match the list at REDESIGN.md:104; `CRAFT.md`:442 has the three render states; `TRANSLATE.md` row 2 explicitly derives the density call.

**BREAKING.md — genuinely citation-free, as claimed. This is the correct outcome.**

- `grep -c '^>' BREAKING.md` → **0**
- Every quoted span in the file is one of: a phrase the file is *criticizing* ("it's more interesting", "it looks generic", "it is what people expect", "it feels more premium", "We are a modern team", "We took some liberties with the layout"), the topic name it says nobody publishes ("when to violate design conventions"), or an internal `§3` reference.
- Zero attribution verbs anywhere (`according to`, `X writes`, `research shows`, `et al` — all absent).
- Only two proper nouns in the file: `GOV.UK` and `Material`, both as examples of a design system in the escape-hatch section, neither quoted.
- Line 15's "the usability literature argues for consistency" is an unsourced characterization of a field, not a quotation, and it's used to explain *why there is nothing to cite*. Not a fabrication.

**No invented citation. The file's premise holds.**

---

# BREAKING.md conditions: real, not platitudes — rule by rule

| Rule | Verdict | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Platform convention** | Real | Names who ("audience uses this daily"), how often ("two seconds × forty times a day"), and where it flips ("a one-visit surface has no compounding term at all"). Plus a budget precondition that enumerates what must be rebuilt (role, name, state, keyboard, focus management, reduced-motion, high-contrast) and a named anti-pattern (the near-miss control). Falsifiable. |
| **Category cliché fence** | Real | The test is stated so it can fail: *can you state what the expected form buys, in this exact place, that the alternatives do not?* — with the failing answer written out ("it is what people expect," no mechanism named = reflex). Plus once-only, plus the position must hold elsewhere. Correctly subordinates itself to row 5. |
| **Density norms** | Real | Both directions get a named population and a countable trigger: page-dense = technical audience comparing, spec table / changelog / pricing matrix; tool-spacious = low-volume high-stakes, "an approval that happens six times a day and cannot be undone." Recording rule demands the count *and* the narrowest-viewport fallback. |
| **Style's own guardrails** | Real, slightly softer | "The purity is doing a job the modified version cannot" is the most subjective condition in the file, but it's backed by a concrete tell: the retroactive-rationale contrast, with both sentences written out so a reviewer can pattern-match. Once-only is checkable. |
| **Two-tier budget** | Strongest in the file | "A stated number, decided in advance" with a worked example ("2.4MB, LCP 3.1s on the target device"), the prototype-first requirement, the art-directed fallback, and an absolute: "on a tool-shaped surface, effectively never." Names units, device, and the never-case. |

No platitudes found. The one general-sounding sentence — "if you cannot write the cost line, you have found a preference" — is a *test*, not a slogan, and the recording rule enforces it ("the cost column cannot be 'none'").

**Carried constraint from Task 4: honored in full.** The never-breakable list (BREAKING.md:271–282) contains all four: `§10`, `§15`, `§16`, and `TRANSLATE.md` row 5. Both upstream promises are now true — `STYLES.md:93` ("Row 5 sits on `BREAKING.md`'s never-breakable list alongside `§10`, `§15`, and `§16`") and `TRANSLATE.md:102–105`. The rationale is the consent distinction, not a list: "These four transfer it onto somebody who did not consent... the line is consent, not magnitude," with the four non-consenting parties named individually. `TRANSLATE.md` independently states the same rationale, so the two files agree.

---

# Ruling on the escalated item: acceptable, but fix one query — don't mark them untested

I executed all four one-liners against a stub DOM rather than eyeballing them.

**Ruling.** Shipping unexecuted read-only DOM queries in a markdown design doc is acceptable. They mutate nothing, fetch nothing, and the blast radius of a wrong one is a wrong number, not a broken site. Marking the block "untested" would be the worse outcome: step 1 is the foundation of the whole method, and an extraction primitive the agent has been told not to trust is an extraction primitive that doesn't get run. Replacing them with prose would be worse still — the file already explains *what* to extract in the table; the code is what makes it reproducible.

**But the report's defense of them is wrong.** "Ordinary DOM API usage and syntactically plain" conflates syntax with semantics. Three of four are correct. The fourth is not, and executing it proves it:

**Important — the palette query does not do what its own two labels claim.** REDESIGN.md:69–73, labelled "the real palette, **ranked** by how often each value is **actually painted**," and in the table as "The real palette, ranked by occurrence."

```js
return [s.color, s.backgroundColor, s.borderTopColor];
```

1. **It double-counts every text color.** `borderTopColor` computes to the element's `color` when no border is set, which is nearly every element. My stub's single H1 — one red text color, zero borders — returned `'rgb(255, 0, 0)': 2`. On a real page, text colors are inflated 2:1 over backgrounds, so the body text color will out-rank the page background even where the background paints a thousand times the area. The output is a census of *computed values*, not of *painted* ones.
2. **It isn't ranked.** The `reduce` returns an insertion-ordered object. A human has to sort it by eye.

Both are one-line fixes: gate the border color on `parseFloat(s.borderTopWidth) > 0`, and append `Object.entries(m).sort((a,b) => b[1]-a[1])`.

This matters more than a normal typo because the ranked palette feeds step 2's "~80% of one family" reading, which is the input to the step-3 fork. And it is the exact failure mode the file itself warns about two paragraphs later: *"Reporting a 44px sweep as a count of WCAG failures is a fabricated finding, and it will be believed."* Same problem, one query up.

---

# Findings

**Critical: none.** No fabricated quotation in either file. BREAKING.md's zero-citation premise verified and intact.

**Important**

1. **`REDESIGN.md:69–73` — the palette one-liner contradicts its own label, twice.** Double-counts text color via the default `borderTopColor`; returns an unsorted object despite "ranked" appearing in both the code comment and the table row. Demonstrated by execution. Two one-line fixes. Full detail above.

**Minor**

2. **`REDESIGN.md:80–83` — the sub-44 sweep's noise sources aren't named.** `getBoundingClientRect()` returns 0×0 for `display:none`, so every closed dropdown, hidden menu item, and unmounted modal control lands in the results; `[tabindex]` additionally catches `tabindex="-1"` programmatic focus targets that aren't interactive. On any real application these will be the *majority* of hits. The "44 is a net, not the law / adjudicate each hit" guard covers this in spirit but doesn't name it, and an agent that doesn't know will report the raw count.

3. **`BREAKING.md:212` — the only non-verbatim quoted string in either file.** Renders `§3`'s requirement as `"what this run did that nobody else does"`; both `PRINCIPLES.md:33-34` and `STYLES.md:516` say *"what it did to the style that nobody else does."* Meaning preserved, internal reference, no fabrication — but it's inside quotation marks and it's the one string that doesn't survive `grep -F`.

4. **`REDESIGN.md:211` — the ladder's gloss contradicts its own rung 7.** "Smallest delta at the highest fiddliness last" is stated as the ordering principle, then rung 7 is "Highest impact on this list and the highest risk." Defensible under impact÷risk (high risk sinks the ratio), but the gloss as written is false for the file's own last rung. One clause fixes it.

5. **`task-9-report.md` — provenance section disagrees with itself on a count.** Line 25 says "four portable JS one-liners I wrote"; line 94 says "the JS one-liners for **these three** are mine"; line 141 says "three portable JS one-liners." Line 94 is the correct one (the fonts query is gstack's, de-`$B`'d). In the section whose entire job is attribution, the count should be consistent.

6. **`scripts/check.sh:52` — the fork check hardcodes five filenames.** `REDESIGN.md` and `BREAKING.md` aren't in the loop, so "both open addressing page-shaped and tool-shaped" is now an unenforced convention for the two newest files. Both do fork correctly — I verified manually — but nothing catches a future regression. Two words in the `for` list.

**Carried risk, verifiable only later (not findings):** the report flags both itself — `REDESIGN.md` asserts `loops/01-direction.md` branches on the classification (Task 10 must build it) and `BREAKING.md` asserts every break gets a `DIRECTION.md` row (whoever specs `DIRECTION.md` must include the table). Same shape as the Task 4 constraint that was honored here. ⚠️ Cannot verify until those tasks land.

**Verdict: Approved with one Important fix.** Land finding 1 before this is treated as final; 2–6 are cleanup. The two files are the strongest pair in the build so far — REDESIGN.md's provenance table makes the seam auditable and it survived a full re-derivation, and BREAKING.md does the hard thing correctly: it is unsourced, says so, and earns its authority from rules that are checkable in-repo rather than from a citation it would have had to invent.

Sequence: set surface class → set platform mode if mobile → run the `ACCESS.md` Loop 1 decisions → derive direction from physical experience (`STYLES.md`) → sample palette from reality in OKLCH → type (two families max) → generate 2–3 concepts → dispatch `surface-designer` → set-level check → **Gate A**.

> **Family pass.** Label each concept with a concrete noun of your own choosing (*exhibition, cockpit, playbill, field-manual*). If two share a label, or a label applies equally to another concept, rework. Do not use a fixed vocabulary for the labels.

**Gate A presents:** rendered images per concept, palette with sampled sources, type system, the collision sentence, and a **SAFE/RISK split with at least two risks**, each with what it costs.

**Rejection diagnosis:** execution vs concept vs brief go to different places. Three rejections at the same gate means the translation table is wrong, not the work.

**CARRIED CONSTRAINT from Task 9 — `DIRECTION.md`'s structure must include a broken-rules table** (rule broken · rationale · cost), because `BREAKING.md`'s recording rule lands against it.

## Verdict

**Spec compliance: ✅** (with one deliberate deviation, ruled correct below)
**Task quality: Approved with findings — 0 Critical, 6 Important, 7 Minor.** All Important items are one-to-three-sentence fixes inside these two files; two of them arguably belong to a later task and are flagged as such.

---

## Spec compliance

Brief Step 1 sequence lands in order, with `§0` prepended: branch → class → platform mode → `ACCESS.md` list → derive → palette → type → concepts → dispatch → set check → Gate A. Step 2 lands in order too. Verified item by item:

| Brief item | Status |
|---|---|
| Swap test + family pass, verbatim, as artifact tests | ✅ `01-direction.md:206–212`, shipped as blockquotes |
| Set-level anti-repeat, conductor-run, thresholds + minimal-brief exemption | ✅ `01-direction.md:256–274`, all three thresholds + the inverse check |
| Aspect ratio keyed to surface class | ✅ `01-direction.md:218–234`, four-row table |
| Announce N, label "Surface X of N" | ✅ `01-direction.md:236–239` |
| Gate A contents incl. SAFE/RISK with ≥2 risks, each costed | ✅ `01-direction.md:280–294` |
| Rejection diagnosis, three destinations + three-rejections rule | ✅ `01-direction.md:320–342` |
| Three-question commercial test per technique | ✅ `02-craft.md:49–62`, with the tool-shaped re-reading |
| Motion spec, both budget tiers as numbers | ✅ `02-craft.md:98–137` |
| `DIRECTION.md` at rendered-style resolution + executable test | ✅ `02-craft.md:141–181`, 25-row schema (report says 24 — trivial miscount) |
| TESTED / PARTIAL / INFERRED | ✅ `02-craft.md:87–96`, each with a written-down example |
| DTCG limits | ✅ `02-craft.md:222–247` — "Community Group Draft of 30 July 2026", explicit "not a W3C Recommendation", `dimension` as `{value, unit}` closed to px/rem, `duration` ms/s, `pt`/`dp`/`sp` inexpressible with `$extensions` escape. Every claim traces to `docs/research/design-tokens-verified.md`, including the honestly-carried "color value shape is unsettled" caveat |

**The five carried constraints — all five landed.**

1. **Redesign branch** — `01-direction.md:44–68`, `§0`, before `§1`. Four-row table, `CURRENT.md` as an input to `§4`, survival list written *before* `§1`. `REDESIGN.md:27` asserts exactly this; the falsifiability rule (`REDESIGN.md:205`) is restated at `01-direction.md:337`. ✅
2. **`STYLES.md` by name** — `01-direction.md:115–117` invokes *"Before the list: derive, don't pick"* then *"Picking one"*, in that order, with the reason. Both are real section headings (`STYLES.md:40`, `:83`). ✅
3. **Broken-rules table in the `DIRECTION.md` schema** — `02-craft.md:180` (schema row) + `:188–204` (its own subsection). ✅
4. **Gate A / Gate B only** — grep for `Gate B1|Gate B2|Gate C|sub-gate` across both files returns nothing. The parents' 2a/2b split became numbered steps. ✅
5. **Anti-shortcut clause + deferral pricing on both gates** — `01-direction.md:296–299` / `:307–316` (5 rows), `02-craft.md:297–300` / `:308–315` (6 rows). Wording matches `PRINCIPLES.md:160–162`. ✅

**Conventions and checks.** `grep -oE '\(§[0-9]+\)' loops/*.md` → empty. Every unbackticked `§N` is either an own-file ref (all carrying above/below except the skip-cost tables, where the file is named in the header) or a foreign-file ref with the file named (`SURFACES.md §1`, `ACCESS.md §13`, `TOOLS.md §13`) — all three verified to exist and to carry the counts claimed (13 + 6 + 4 in `ACCESS.md`; nine in `TOOLS.md`). Both files open on `## The fork`. Six markdown links, all resolving; everything unbuilt (`AGENTS.md`, `agents/*`, `skills/`) is backticked only. `./scripts/check.sh` reproduces the report exactly: 9 failures, all "missing file" from Tasks 12–14, zero new. The `tokens.json` example parses. ✅

---

## The escalated call: **the deviation was correct**

`BREAKING.md:310–314` ships a four-column table — rule broken · what it buys · what it costs · why the trade is honest here — with three worked example rows, and `:308` says "every break gets one row **in `DIRECTION.md`**". The loop reproduces that header exactly and reuses `BREAKING.md`'s first worked row verbatim (`02-craft.md:194–196`).

Shipping the brief's three columns would have (a) orphaned `BREAKING.md`'s fourth column, which is the column carrying the actual argument, (b) made `BREAKING.md`'s own three worked examples unpasteable into the file they are specified to land in, and (c) left `BREAKING.md` — already shipped and already asserting this — lying. The brief's three columns read as a paraphrase of `BREAKING.md`, not an independent requirement. The implementer also carried the three properties and the four never-breakable rules (`02-craft.md:198–204`), so nothing from `BREAKING.md` dangles. Correct call, correctly reasoned.

---

## Important findings

**1. `N` is undefined once there are 2–3 concepts.** `01-direction.md:236` announces *"nine surfaces, nine images"*; `:243` dispatches *"one agent per surface, one image each"*; Gate A at `:283` presents *"the rendered images, **per concept**, all N of them"*. So is N nine, or twenty-seven? The label format `"Surface X of N"` has no concept slot, so under the 3×N reading three images collide on the same label. An agent must invent either the count or the labelling scheme, and the cost difference is 3×. Inherited from the parents (`portfolio.me/loops/02-design.md:80` vs `:88` has the identical hole) — but the whole point of this file was fixing inherited image-generation bugs. One sentence in `§8` fixes it.

**2. The set-level check compares a vocabulary that does not exist.** `§10` rejects a set when the same *composition anchor* repeats twice running or the same *background mode* three times. You are implementing Task 11 of the `inter.face` build: the two worker agent specs. inter.face is a cross-agent design plugin made of markdown; an agent reads it and follows it, there is no runtime.

Working directory: `/Users/taha/Documents/inter.face` (git branch `build/plugin-files`).

**Read this first — your requirements:**
`.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-01-inter-face-build/task-11-brief.md`

**Read what dispatches you:** `loops/01-direction.md` (§8/§9 dispatch `surface-designer`), `loops/02-craft.md` (dispatches `technique-prototyper`). **Read what you must obey:** `PRINCIPLES.md`, `SURFACES.md`, `CRAFT.md`, `STYLES.md`.
**Mine for craft rules:** `docs/audit/competitor-imagegen.md`.

Create `agents/surface-designer.md` and `agents/technique-prototyper.md`, each with YAML frontmatter (`name`, `description`) matching the pattern in `/Users/taha/Documents/portfolio.me/agents/section-designer.md`.

---

## `agents/surface-designer.md`

One agent per surface **per concept**, one image each, never a compressed board — *a compressed board hides exactly the detail the human needs to judge.*

**CARRIED CONSTRAINT — you must close a gap the loops depend on.** `loops/01-direction.md` §10 runs a set-level anti-repeat check that rejects a set when *"the same composition anchor repeats more than twice running"* or *"the same background mode three times"*. **Neither term is defined anywhere in this repo.** With free-form labels chosen independently by parallel workers, that check is unfalsifiable and passes vacuously.

So: **define both vocabularies here, as closed menus**, and require each worker to log one pick from each. `docs/audit/competitor-imagegen.md` (search for "composition anchor" and "background mode") has the source menus — use them, adapt to cover tool-shaped surfaces too. A closed menu is what makes the loop's check able to fail. This is the single most important thing in this task.

**Also required:**
- **Platform mode** honored (iOS / Android / cross-platform-neutral) per `SURFACES.md`.
- **Safe-area bands** — every mobile surface image shows or reserves four bands: status, title/nav, content, bottom-nav/home-indicator. *A screen running edge-to-edge in all four directions has failed regardless of how it looks.*
- **Aspect ratio** taken from `loops/01-direction.md`'s per-class table — do not restate a different number.
- **Text-in-image constraints** per `PRINCIPLES.md` `§9`: realistic copy lengths, minimal text per image, no invented brand names, no placeholder superlatives.
- **Device framing inverted from the source skill's default:** bare screen unless physicality is load-bearing. A phone bezel eats ~30% of the canvas and pulls the model's fidelity toward rendering a handset instead of the interface under review.
- **Embarrassment self-gate** before returning: would a designer put their name on this? Reject in the worker — cheaper than at Gate A.
- The **return contract**: the image, plus the logged composition anchor and background mode.

## `agents/technique-prototyper.md`

One agent per technique. Delivers a standalone runnable HTML file, a screenshot, a **measured** frame rate under load, the byte cost, all required states for the surface class (three render states page-shaped; the nine data states are `TOOLS.md`'s and belong to the build, not the prototype), and a verdict — **ship / cut / ship-with-caveat** — carrying a **TESTED / PARTIAL / INFERRED** evidence label per `loops/02-craft.md`.

Free rein while prototyping (any library, any CDN); that freedom ends at handoff where `§7` requires everything vendored.

**Report failure honestly — failing cheap here is the entire point of the loop.** A rejected prototype is never argued into acceptance, tuned during the build, or carried forward on the theory that it comes together in integration.

---

**Conventions:** both files must address **page-shaped** and **tool-shaped**. Backticked `` `§N` `` = a `PRINCIPLES.md` rule; own-section refs take above/below, never bare `(§N)`. Markdown links to files that exist are fine; `AGENTS.md`, `skills/`, `commands/` do not exist yet — backticks only. State that an agent which cannot spawn subagents reads the file and does the work inline. No placeholders.

**Steps:** read → write both → run `./scripts/check.sh` (no new failures, no placeholder hits, links resolve) → commit both with the brief's message.

**Report contract:** full report to `.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-01-inter-face-build/task-11-report.md` — what you shipped, **the two closed menus you defined and where each term came from**, and the check output.

Return ONLY: status, commit SHA, one-line check summary, concerns.
